title: CNF, DNF & K-maps
eyebrow: COMP9020 · Week 2 · Normal forms and Karnaugh maps
goal: Recognise and produce CNF and DNF, write the canonical DNF from a truth table, and read an optimal expression off a 3- or 4-variable Karnaugh map.
magic: DNF: OR of AND-blocks. CNF: AND of OR-blocks. `′` only on letters.
Convert: arrows out → negations down → distribute.
Canonical DNF: one full product per 1-row.
K-map order `yz, yz′, y′z′, y′z`; edges wrap; the four corners touch.
Fewest, largest rectangles of 1/2/4/8; never cover a blank; keep the unchanging letters.

blocks.title: 💡 Learn it, one idea at a time
Literals, clauses, CNF and DNF
blocks.summary: DNF = a sum of products (OR of ANDs). CNF = a product of sums (AND of ORs). Only one level of nesting.
blocks.picture: A restaurant rule in DNF: "(burger AND fries) OR (salad AND soup)": a list of complete combos, any one works. In CNF: "(burger OR salad) AND (fries OR soup)": a list of requirements, all must hold.
blocks.official: A **literal** is `p` or `p′` (Week 2, slide 58). **CNF**: a product `∏ Cᵢ` where each clause `Cᵢ` is a **sum** of literals, e.g. `p + q + r′`. **DNF**: a sum `∑ Cᵢ` where each clause is a **product** of literals, e.g. `pqr′`. A clause can be a single literal. No deeper nesting allowed (slide 59). So `p + q′` is CNF (1 clause) and DNF (2 clauses); `rs′t′` is CNF (3 clauses) and DNF (1 clause).

steps: `(a + b′)(a′ + c)`: a product of two sums of literals → **CNF** (2 clauses).
`ab′ + c`: a sum of two products of literals (`c` is a one-literal product) → **DNF**.
`(ab)′`: the `′` sits on a product, not on a single letter → **neither** (push it in first: `a′ + b′`, which is both).

tries.q: Is `x′ + y + z` in CNF, DNF, both or neither?
tries.why: CNF with one clause `(x′ + y + z)`; DNF with three one-literal clauses.

tries.q: Is `(a + b)c + d` in CNF, DNF, both or neither?
tries.why: `(a + b)c` has a sum nested inside a product, inside a sum: too deep. Expand: `ac + bc + d` (DNF).

tries.q: Is `pq′r` in CNF, DNF, both or neither?
tries.why: DNF with one clause; CNF with three one-literal clauses.

tries.q: Is `(p + q)(r + s′)(t)` in CNF?
tries.why: Every factor is a sum of literals.

trap.tempting: `(ab)′` is fine in a DNF because it only has literals in it.
trap.correct: In CNF/DNF, `′` may only sit on a **single letter**. `(ab)′` must first become `a′ + b′`.
trap.test: Look for a `′` after a bracket. If there is one, it's not in normal form yet.

blocks.magic: DNF: OR of AND-blocks. CNF: AND of OR-blocks. `′` only on letters.

blocks.title: Converting any expression to CNF or DNF
blocks.summary: Remove `⇒`/`⇔`, push `′` down to the letters, then distribute.
blocks.picture: Like refactoring nested `if`s into a flat list of cases (DNF) or a flat list of guard checks (CNF).
blocks.official: **Theorem** (Week 2, slide 60): every Boolean expression has an equivalent CNF and an equivalent DNF. Method (slides 60–61): (0) eliminate `⇒` with `A ⇒ B ≡ ¬A ∨ B` (and `⇔` with its definition); (1) push negations down to the atoms with De Morgan and double negation; (2) distribute: `x + (y₁ · … · yₙ) = (x + y₁) · … · (x + yₙ)` for CNF, `x(y₁ + … + yₙ) = xy₁ + … + xyₙ` for DNF. The lecture's example turns `¬(¬p ∧ ((r ∧ s) ⇒ q))` into the CNF `(p + r)(p + s)(p + q′)`.

watch.q: Convert `(p ⇒ q) ⇒ r` to DNF, then to CNF.
steps: Push `¬` in (De Morgan): `(p ∧ ¬q) ∨ r`, i.e. `pq′ + r`. That's **DNF**.
For CNF, distribute `r +` over the product: `(p + r)(q′ + r)`.

tries.q: Convert `¬(p ∨ (q ∧ ¬r))` to CNF.
tries.why: De Morgan: `p′ · (qr′)′` = `p′(q′ + r)`. Two clauses: `p′` and `q′ + r`.

tries.q: Convert the same `¬(p ∨ (q ∧ ¬r))` to DNF.
tries.why: Distribute `p′` over `(q′ + r)`.

tries.q: Write `p ⇔ q` in DNF and in CNF.
tries.why: DNF: both true or both false. CNF: `(p ⇒ q) ∧ (q ⇒ p)` with each arrow as a sum.

tries.q: Convert `(a + b)(c + d)` to DNF.
tries.why: Multiply out every pair, like `(a + b)(c + d)` in school algebra.

trap.tempting: Distribute first, deal with the `′`s later.
trap.correct: Push every `′` down to the letters **first**. Distributing over a negated bracket gives wrong results.
trap.test: Before distributing, scan for `′` after a bracket. None left? Now distribute.

blocks.title: Canonical DNF: one product per true row
blocks.summary: Read the truth table: every row with output 1 becomes one full product of literals. OR them together.
blocks.picture: A guest list written in full: instead of "everyone from marketing", you list every single allowed person. Long, but uniquely determined by the rule.
blocks.official: For an assignment `π`, let `ℓᵢ = xᵢ` if `π(xᵢ) = 1` and `ℓᵢ = xᵢ′` if `π(xᵢ) = 0`, and `t_π = ℓ₁ · … · ℓₙ` (Week 2, slide 62). The **canonical DNF** is `E^dnf = ∑_{E(π) = 1} t_π` (every true row, every variable in every term). To expand a shorter term, multiply by `(z + z′)` for each missing variable (slide 65: `xy = xy(z + z′) = xyz + xyz′`). Example (slide 63): the table with outputs 1, 0, 1, 1 for `xy` = 00, 01, 10, 11 gives `x′y′ + xy′ + xy`, which simplifies to `x + y′`.

watch.q: Find the canonical DNF of `E` where `E = 1` exactly for `(x, y)` = `(0, 1)`, `(1, 0)`, `(1, 1)`.

tries.q: Canonical DNF of `x′z` in the variables `x, y, z`?
tries.why: Multiply by `(y + y′)`: `x′z(y + y′)`.

tries.q: Canonical DNF of `y` in the variables `x, y, z`? How many terms?
tries.why: Two missing variables → `2² = 4` full products.

tries.q: Canonical DNF of `x′z + y` in `x, y, z`? How many terms?
tries.why: `y` gives the 4 rows with `y = 1`. `x′z` gives `x′yz` (already there) and `x′y′z` (new). One term per true row.

tries.q: How many terms does the canonical DNF of `0` have? And of `1` (in 3 variables)?
tries.a: **0 terms** (the empty sum is 0) and **8 terms** (every row is true).
tries.why: One term per true row.

trap.tempting: The canonical DNF is the shortest DNF.
trap.correct: Canonical = **every** true row written out in full. It's usually long; the shortest form comes from simplifying (or a K-map).
trap.test: Count: canonical DNF terms = number of 1-rows in the table.

blocks.title: Karnaugh maps: the truth table folded so neighbours differ by one letter
blocks.summary: Columns go `yz, yz′, y′z′, y′z`: each step changes exactly one letter, and the ends wrap around.
blocks.picture: Seats around a round table: everyone has two neighbours, including the first and last seats, which are next to each other.
blocks.official: For `k = 2, 3, 4` variables, a K-map is a rectangle of `2ᵏ` cells, one per row of the truth table (Week 2, slide 66). The slides order the columns `yz, yz′, y′z′, y′z` and, for 4 variables, the rows `wx, wx′, w′x′, w′x`. Neighbouring cells differ in **one** letter, and the map is a **torus**: the left edge touches the right edge, and the top touches the bottom (slide 67). Mark the cells where the function is 1 with `+`.

watch.q: Where do the `+`s go for `x′y′z + xyz′`?
watch.answer: Two `+`s: row `x′` / column `y′z`, and row `x` / column `yz′`.

tries.q: In the 3-variable map, which cells are neighbours of `x′yz′` (row `x′`, column `yz′`)?
tries.why: Each neighbour changes exactly one letter: `x`, `z`, or `y`.

tries.q: Are the columns `yz` and `y′z` neighbours?
tries.why: They differ only in `y`. The map wraps: the first and last columns are adjacent.

tries.q: Why is the column order `yz, yz′, y′z′, y′z` and not the binary order `yz, yz′, y′z, y′z′`?
tries.a: So that every step changes **one** letter. In binary order, `yz′ → y′z` changes both `y` and `z`, and neighbours could no longer be merged.
tries.why: This one-letter-at-a-time order is a Gray code.

trap.tempting: Write the columns in binary order `11, 10, 01, 00`.
trap.correct: Use the one-change order (slide 66): `yz, yz′, y′z′, y′z` = `11, 10, 00, 01`.
trap.test: Read neighbouring labels: exactly one letter should flip.

blocks.magic: Neighbour = one letter different. Edges wrap.

blocks.title: Cover the `+`s with the fewest, largest rectangles
blocks.summary: Rectangles of 1, 2, 4 or 8 cells, never covering a blank, as large as possible, as few as possible. Each rectangle gives one product.
blocks.picture: Covering spilled paint with rectangular stickers: use the biggest stickers you can, as few as possible, and never cover the clean floor.
blocks.official: Rules (Week 2, slide 67): cover every `+` cell; **never** cover an empty cell (those are 0s); rectangles have sides of 1, 2 or 4 cells (3 adjacent cells are useless); they may wrap around the edges; each must be as large as possible; use as few as possible. A rectangle's product keeps only the letters that are **constant** across it. Lecture exercise (slide 67): the map with `+` at `xyz, xyz′, xy′z, x′yz, x′y′z′, x′y′z` gives `f = xy + x′y′ + z`.

watch.q: Read this map: `+` at row `x`: `y′z′`, `y′z`; row `x′`: `yz`, `y′z`.
steps: Row `x`, columns `y′z′`, `y′z`: a 1×2 rectangle. Constant: `x`, `y′`. Product `xy′`.
Row `x′`, columns `yz` and `y′z`: they touch around the edge. Constant: `x′`, `z`. Product `x′z`.
Could one rectangle be bigger? A 2×2 would need blank cells. No.

tries.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
tries.why: The four `z` cells (columns `yz` and `y′z`, which wrap) form a 2×2 block: `z`. The last `+` (`xyz′`) pairs with `xyz` to its left: `xy`.

tries.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
tries.why: Row `x`: `yz′`, `y′z′` side by side → `xz′`. Row `x′`: `yz` and `y′z` wrap around → `x′z`. (It's `x ⊕ z`.)
tries.wrong: If you wrote four separate products: the `x′` cells are neighbours across the edge.

tries.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
tries.why: The four `z′` cells (the two middle columns) form a 2×2 block: `z′`. The `+` at `xyz` pairs with `xyz′`: `xy`.

trap.tempting: A rectangle of 3 cells in a row is fine.
trap.correct: Sides must be 1, 2 or 4. Three `+`s in a row need two overlapping rectangles of 2.
trap.test: Count each side of every rectangle: 1, 2 or 4 only.

blocks.magic: Biggest legal rectangles, fewest of them; keep the letters that don't change.

blocks.title: Four variables: a 4×4 map that wraps both ways
blocks.summary: Rows `wx, wx′, w′x′, w′x`, columns `yz, yz′, y′z′, y′z`. Rectangles of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16; the four corners are one block.
blocks.picture: A world map on a doughnut: walk off the right edge and you appear on the left; walk off the top and you appear at the bottom. The four corners all touch.
blocks.official: Same rules with 16 cells (Week 2, slides 69–70: 10.6.6(c)). A block of 4 kills 2 letters, a block of 8 kills 3. The **four corners** are adjacent (they differ in one letter pairwise around the torus), so they form one block of 4.

watch.q: Read this 4-variable map: `+` in columns `y′z` (all four rows) and in rows `wx`, `wx′` at columns `yz`, `yz′`.
steps: Column `y′z`, all rows: a 4×1 block. Constant: `y′`, `z` → `y′z`.
Every `+` is covered; no blank is.

tries.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
tries.why: Rows `wx`, `w′x` (they wrap top–bottom) × columns `yz`, `y′z` (they wrap left–right): the **four corners**, a block of 4 → `xz`. The middle 2×2 (rows `wx′`, `w′x′` × columns `yz′`, `y′z′`) → `x′z′`.

check.g: BA:wxyz + wxy′z + wx′yz′ + wx′y′z′ + w′xyz + w′xy′z + w′x′yz′ + w′x′y′z′

tries.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
tries.why: Rows `wx`, `w′x` (wrap) × columns `yz′`, `y′z′` → block of 4, constant `x`, `z′` → `xz′`. The two `+`s in column `yz`, rows `wx′`, `w′x′` → `x′yz`.

check.g: BA:wxyz′ + wxy′z′ + wx′yz + w′xyz′ + w′xy′z′ + w′x′yz

trap.tempting: Corners are far apart, so they can't be grouped.
trap.correct: The map wraps both ways, so the four corners are mutual neighbours and form one block of 4.
trap.test: Check the labels: corner cells differ by one letter from their wrap-around neighbours.

blocks.magic: A block of 2ᵐ cells removes `m` letters. Corners touch.

items.q: A rectangle covers the cells `xyz′` and `xy′z′`. Its product?
items.why: `y` changes, so it drops out; `x` and `z′` stay.

items.q: A 2×2 block covers `xyz, xy′z, x′yz, x′y′z`. Its product?
items.why: `x` and `y` both change; only `z` is constant.

items.q: Is `a′b + c′` in DNF?
items.why: A sum of products of literals (`c′` is a one-literal product).

items.q: Is `(a + b)′c` in CNF?
items.why: `(a + b)′` puts `′` on a bracket. Pushed in: `a′b′c`, which is both CNF and DNF.

items.q: How many cells in a 4-variable K-map?
How many terms in the canonical DNF of `xy′` (variables `x, y, z`)?
items.why: One missing variable → 2 terms.

items.q: Convert `(a ⇒ b) ∧ (b ⇒ c)` to CNF.
items.why: Each arrow becomes a sum; the `∧` is already the top level.

items.q: Convert `(a ⇒ b) ∧ (b ⇒ c)` to DNF (then drop any `0` terms).
items.why: Multiply out: `a′b′ + a′c + bb′ + bc`, and `bb′ = 0`. (`a′c` is even redundant by consensus: `a′b′ + bc` is enough.)

items.q: Canonical DNF of the function that is 1 exactly on the rows `(x, y, z)` = `(1, 1, 0)`, `(0, 0, 1)`, `(0, 1, 1)`.
items.why: One full product per 1-row: `1 → x`, `0 → x′`, and so on.

items.q: Simplify that canonical DNF `xyz′ + x′y′z + x′yz`.
items.why: `x′y′z + x′yz = x′z` (opposites). `xyz′` has no partner.

items.q: Convert `¬(a ⇔ b)` to DNF.
items.why: Exactly one of them is true.

blocks.sub: Exam style: read an optimal expression off a K-map (like the lecture's 10.4.2 and 10.6.6(c)). All maps are original.

items.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
items.why: The whole `x′` row (4 cells) → `x′`. The remaining `+` at `xy′z` pairs with `x′y′z` below it → `y′z`.

items.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
items.why: Columns `yz`, `yz′` in both rows → `y`. The `+` at `xy′z′` pairs with `xyz′` → `xz′`.

items.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
items.why: Row `x`, columns `yz`, `yz′` → `xy`. Row `x′`, columns `y′z′`, `y′z` → `x′y′`. No 2×2 is possible.

items.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
items.why: The whole `wx` row → `wx`. The whole `yz` column → `yz`. They overlap at `wxyz`, which is allowed.

check.g: BA:wxyz + wxyz′ + wxy′z + wxy′z′ + wx′yz + w′xyz + w′x′yz

items.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
items.why: Rows `wx`, `wx′` × columns `y′z′`, `y′z` → `wy′`. Rows `w′x′`, `w′x` in column `yz′` → `w′yz′`.

check.g: BA:wxy′z + wxy′z′ + wx′y′z + wx′y′z′ + w′xyz′ + w′x′yz′

items.q: Find the optimal expression for this map (fewest, largest rectangles).
items.why: Rows `wx`, `w′x` (wrap top–bottom) × columns `yz`, `y′z` (wrap left–right) → the four corners → `xz`. Row `w′x′`, columns `yz′`, `y′z′` → `w′x′z′`.

check.g: BA:wxyz + wxy′z + w′xyz + w′xy′z + w′x′yz′ + w′x′y′z′

items.q: Find an optimal expression for this map. Is the answer unique?
items.a: **Two optimal answers:** `xy + xz′ + x′y′` and `xy + y′z′ + x′y′`. Both use 3 rectangles of 2.
items.why: `xy` and `x′y′` are forced. The last `+` (`xy′z′`) can join `xyz′` (giving `xz′`) or `x′y′z′` (giving `y′z′`). Minimal forms need not be unique.

items.q: Find an optimal expression for this 4-variable map.
items.why: Row `w′x′` (all 4) → `w′x′`. Rows `wx′`, `w′x′` × columns `yz′`, `y′z′` → `x′z′`. The lone `+` at `wxyz` has no `+` neighbour, so it stays a full product.

check.g: BA:wxyz + wx′yz′ + wx′y′z′ + w′x′yz + w′x′yz′ + w′x′y′z + w′x′y′z′

items.q: Find an optimal expression for this map. How much shorter than the canonical DNF is it?
items.a: **`x′y′ + x′z′ + y′z′ + xyz`**: 4 terms instead of 5 (and 9 literals instead of 15).
items.why: The three pairs overlap at `x′y′z′`. `xyz` has no `+` neighbour. The function is "at most one of `x, y, z` is true, or all three are".

items.q: Why is covering an empty (0) cell never allowed, even if it makes a bigger rectangle?
items.a: Every cell a rectangle covers becomes a 1 of the resulting expression. Covering a 0 changes the function.
items.why: Bigger is only better among rectangles that stay inside the `+` cells.

items.q: Convert `(p ⇔ q) ⇒ r` to CNF.
items.why: `≡ ¬(p ⇔ q) ∨ r ≡ (pq′ + p′q) + r`. For CNF: `pq′ + p′q = (p + q)(p′ + q′)`, then distribute `+ r` into each clause.

items.q: CNF, DNF, both or neither: `a + b′c`?
Canonical DNF of `x′` in `x, y`?
Allowed rectangle sides in a K-map?
Optimal expression for `+` at `xyz′`, `x′yz′`, `xy′z′`, `x′y′z′` (the two middle columns)?

lines: Literal = `p` or `p′`. CNF = `∏(sums of literals)`, DNF = `∑(products of literals)`; one-literal clauses allowed.
Every expression has a CNF and a DNF: eliminate `⇒`, push `′` in, distribute.
Canonical DNF: a full product for each 1-row; expand short terms with `(z + z′)`.
K-maps: Gray order, wrap-around torus, rectangles of 1/2/4 per side, maximal and few, no 0s.
Block of `2ᵐ` cells → a product with `m` fewer letters. Optimal forms are not always unique.
